title: Your Next Move
titleHtml: Your next move, planned on purpose.
tagline: Using the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal to plan your own growth and next internal move.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: point the talent systems you already know at your own career, name the direction you want next, and treat an internal move as a career path the university wants you to take.
heroLead: You already know the tools. Today you point the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal at your own career: a named direction and a move you would say yes to.
objectives: Use the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal together to plan your own growth and next move
Name a specific direction and bring your skills profile current enough to match it
Treat an internal move as a normal, encouraged Vanderbilt career path
missionTie: Destination Vanderbilt means people choose to come here, and a staff member with a real plan for their next internal move keeps choosing to stay.

agenda.d: What the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal each do for your own plan.
The current profile and the named direction that let the matching work for you.
Retiring the old myths about applying internally at Vanderbilt.

manifesto: You know the tools. Now point them at your own next move.

sections.headline: Point the tools at your own career.
sections.lead: Earlier in the series you learned the Transfer Portal as a system. Now point it at your own career. Deloitte's work on internal talent marketplaces names the payoff: people get matched to work by skills and aspiration, not by luck.
sections.group: In pairs: what do you want these systems working on for you this year, a skill, a project, a move? One pair shares.
sections.solo: Write down what you want these systems working on for you this year: a skill, a project, or a move.

card.text: Read the two systems as one kit. The Talent Marketplace grows you where you are, through your skills profile and stretch work. The Transfer Portal carries the move once you are ready. A real plan uses both, in that order.

interaction.context: Everyone in this room already knows the Transfer Portal; the series taught it in depth. What most people have never done is sit down with the Marketplace and the Portal open and ask the selfish question: what is my plan? Today is that hour, with the university's explicit blessing.
interaction.discuss: When you learned the Portal earlier in the series, what did you privately wonder about your own next move? Say the honest version out loud.
interaction.q: Quick check: you want a growth plan, not just a job search. Where does it start?

opts.t: Watching the Transfer Portal until a role you like appears
opts.why: That is a job search with extra steps. Roles are the last mile; the plan starts with the skills and direction that make a role a fit.

opts.t: A current skills profile and a named direction in the Talent Marketplace
opts.why: Exactly. The Marketplace grows you toward the direction you named, and by the time a Portal role fits, you are ready for it.

opts.t: Waiting for your manager to build a development plan for you
opts.why: Managers coach and advocate, and the plan is yours. Nobody else can name the direction you would say yes to.

deeper.title: Growth first, move second
deeper.body: The commonest planning mistake is starting with a destination role and working backward. Roles change, get frozen, or go to someone readier. Directions are sturdier than destinations: name the kind of work and the skills it runs on, then let the Marketplace grow you toward it while the Portal watches for openings shaped like it. When a role finally surfaces, you are applying from readiness instead of hope.
steps: Write your direction as one sentence: the kind of work, not a job title. Test it: would three different real roles fit inside it?
List the two skills that direction runs on which you cannot evidence yet. Those are your Marketplace growth targets.
Open the Transfer Portal once this week and note which current openings rhyme with your direction, even ones you are not ready for.

sections.headline: Write a profile the matching can read.
sections.lead: Matching is only as good as what it can read. Two moves keep you findable: a Talent Marketplace profile that says what you can actually do, and a direction named in writing. Build both here.

interaction.intro: Two entries decide what the matching can see. Choose how you write your skills and how you name your direction.

opts.t: Copy the duties list from your job description.
opts.coach: The systems already know your job exists. Duties describe the role; the matching needs the skills, including the ones your role never uses.

opts.t: List your strongest skills from this role only.
opts.coach: Good start, half the picture. Skills from past roles, volunteer work, and side projects match real openings too. Claim all of it.

opts.t: List every skill you can actually use, from any role, with a line on how you have used it.
opts.coach: Full inventory plus evidence. The how-I-used-it line is what turns a keyword into a credible match.

opts.t: Leave it blank; you don't want to seem restless.
opts.coach: A blank field gives the matching nowhere to aim. Naming a direction signals ambition, and Vanderbilt is asking for exactly that signal.

opts.t: Write something broad like 'open to opportunities.'
opts.coach: Broad interest matches everything, which means it matches nothing well. The matching can act on 'project work in student-facing units'; it cannot act on 'open.'

opts.t: Name a direction: the kind of work, the skills you want to grow, what you would say yes to.
opts.coach: Specific and forward-looking. This is the entry that surfaces a stretch project before it is posted anywhere.

heads.strong: Findable. Your profile gives the matching real material, and the surfaced fits will look like you on your best day.
heads.mid: Partially visible. The systems can see the role you have; they still cannot see the person you are.
heads.weak: Invisible. The matching has nothing to read, so the opportunities will keep going to people who wrote things down.

reactions.strong: A few weeks later, a project in another school surfaces on your dashboard, matched to a skill your current role never uses. It looks interesting. It found you.
reactions.mid: The matches that surface look a lot like your current job in different buildings. Accurate, and underwhelming. The missing half of your profile was the interesting half.
reactions.weak: Months pass. A colleague with your exact skills gets surfaced for a project you would have loved. The difference between you was a written-down profile.

deeper.title: The evidence line
deeper.body: A skill without an evidence line is a keyword, and keywords are cheap. The strongest lines have three parts: what you did, the scale or the stakes, and what it produced. 'Process mapping: redesigned intake during our busiest cycle and cleared the backlog' is credible, findable, and easy for an advocate to repeat. Skills from past roles count in full; the matching has no way to discount where a capability came from.
steps: Take your three strongest skills and write the three-part evidence line for each: the thing, the stakes, the result.
Add one skill from a past role or outside work that your current job never uses, with its own evidence line.
Read each line as a stranger. If it could describe anyone with your title, sharpen it until it could only describe you.

sections.headline: An internal move is a career path.
sections.lead: Hear the policy plainly: internal mobility is a normal, encouraged career path at Vanderbilt. LinkedIn's research finds people stay nearly twice as long where moving inside is easy.

source.label: Internal mobility and retention, LinkedIn Workplace Learning research

sections.group: In pairs: what have you heard, in any workplace, about what happens to people who apply internally? Myth or real, 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Write down one thing you have believed about applying internally. After this section, decide: myth or real?

interaction.intro: Sort each statement: an old myth to retire, a normal move to support, or a readiness gap to fix. Ask what each one would do to a real career.
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. Retire the myths out loud; they only survive in silence.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: a myth punishes ambition. A normal move grows a career inside Vanderbilt, and a readiness gap is just a profile nobody wrote yet.

items.q: 'Don't let your manager see you looking at internal postings. They'll take it personally.'
items.why: This is the myth the Transfer Portal is built to kill. A move inside Vanderbilt keeps the talent here, and managers are measured on growing people, never on holding them.

items.q: An advisor sees a program role in another college that fits their skills, tells their manager, and applies.
items.why: This is the path working as designed. The manager conversation is a courtesy and a coaching chance; the application needs nobody's permission.

items.q: A financial analyst wants project work badly, but their profile lists nothing beyond their current job title.
items.why: No myth and no move here, just a matching engine with nothing to read. One honest hour on the profile fixes it.

deeper.title: The manager conversation, scripted
deeper.body: The myths mostly die in one specific conversation: telling your manager you are looking at a move. Plan it in three beats. The direction: what you are growing toward and why. The timing: nothing is decided, you are being deliberate, not restless. The continuity: what you would do to land your current work well. Managers who hear all three usually turn into advocates, because you have just shown them exactly how to support you.
steps: Draft the three beats for your own manager conversation: direction, timing, continuity. Two sentences each.
Say the direction beat out loud once. If it sounds like an apology, rewrite it until it sounds like a plan.

recap.q: How do the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal fit together in your plan?
opts: They are two names for the same system
The Marketplace grows you; the Portal carries the move when you are ready
The Portal is for managers; the Marketplace is for staff
You pick one and ignore the other
recap.why: One kit, two jobs: grow where you are through the Marketplace, move when ready through the Portal. A plan uses both, and starts with the growing.

recap.q: What makes a skills profile genuinely findable?
opts: A copy of your job description
All your usable skills, any role, with how you used them
Only skills your manager has signed off on
Keeping it short so it is easy to read
recap.why: Full inventory plus evidence, past roles included. The interesting matches usually come from the skills your current job never uses.

recap.q: A colleague applies for an internal role in another school. What is that at Vanderbilt?
opts: A risky move to keep quiet
recap.why: Internal mobility keeps talent inside the university, which is the point of Goal 1. Managers coach the move; they never gate the application.

recapMsgs.high: The plan is in reach. Now write the profile and the direction down for real.
recapMsgs.mid: Close. The findability section is worth one more look before you build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One move that starts the plan.
capstone.lead: Pick the move that starts your plan. Your own words, your own career; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: What direction is this plan about? The kind of work or growth you would say yes to.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. student-facing project work; growing toward process improvement lead

practices.name: The skills sweep
practices.move: Spend one honest hour bringing your Talent Marketplace profile current: every usable skill, any role, one evidence line each.

practices.name: The named direction
practices.move: Write the direction you would say yes to: the kind of work, the skills you want to grow. Then bring it to your manager.

practices.name: The Portal scan
practices.move: Browse the Transfer Portal once, on purpose, and note one role or project that rhymes with your direction and why.

whens.out: The move happens this week, done by Friday.
You bring it to your next 1:1: here is my direction, and here is the plan I am starting.
The move happens within two weeks, with the hour already blocked on your calendar.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what direction did you name, and what surprised you writing it down?

closing.headline: Start the plan this week.
closing.lead: Make the move on your card this week: the profile hour, the named direction, or the Portal scan. Thursday's session covers advocacy, the other half of moving inside Vanderbilt.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Make the move on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it as built: one honest hour, one named direction, or one deliberate Portal scan. Curious what makes people stay and grow? This month's LinkedIn Learning pick, Retaining Your Best Talent by Roberta Matuson, comes with a navigator-led stay-interview practice lab.
closing.brandline: Write the direction down this week.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no management experience assumed. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. Builds on the Transfer Portal month earlier in the series; February is the Retain, Grow, Move month on succession and internal mobility.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the move on your card happen? What direction did you name? What did your profile claim that your title never showed?' Count of started next-move plans is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: The tools, pointed at you
s1.purpose: Reconnect the room to the two talent systems and turn them from things people know into a personal planning kit.
s1.say: You already know the Transfer Portal; the series spent a whole month on it. Today we get selfish with it. The Talent Marketplace holds your skills and surfaces growth work; the Portal carries the internal moves. Most people learn tools like these and never once point them at their own career. Deloitte's research on internal talent marketplaces makes the case plainly: when skills and aspirations are visible, people get matched to work instead of waiting to be noticed. That is the whole agenda today: your own growth, planned on purpose.
facilitate: Read the concept card once; the two-jobs split is the whole slide.
Show the In the room card, then open the discussion prompt: what did you privately wonder about your own next move? Take two or three voices.
Run the breakout: what do you want these systems working on for you this year?

ask.q: What is the difference between watching the Portal and having a plan?
expect: Watching is passive; a plan has a direction
A plan includes growth before the move
ask.respond: Right. Watching waits for luck. A plan names a direction, grows toward it in the Marketplace, and lets the Portal handle the last mile.

s1.debrief: The systems are one kit: grow where you are, move when you are ready. The whole game is the direction you name, which is where section two goes.
s1.watchFor: System how-to questions pulling the session into mechanics. Park them: the Portal month covered the how; today is what you do with it.
s1.transition: So the plan runs on your profile and your direction. Time to build both.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; take answers to the discussion prompt in chat.

s2.title: Getting findable
s2.purpose: Get every person to draft a full skills entry and a specific named direction in the Talent Marketplace.
s2.say: The matching can only read what you wrote down. A profile that copies your job description makes you findable for the job you already have. The skills sweep and the named direction make you findable for the work you want next. And the skills your current role never uses are exactly where the interesting matches come from.
facilitate: Run Build your findability; two minutes for both choices, then run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: full inventory with evidence, one specific direction.

ask.q: Why do people leave the direction field blank?
expect: Fear of seeming disloyal or restless
Honestly not knowing what they want yet
ask.respond: That first fear is exactly what section three retires. For the second: name whatever is true this year. A draft direction beats a blank every time.

s2.debrief: Findable is a choice: every usable skill with evidence, one specific direction. Blank fields match nothing.
s2.watchFor: People underclaiming, especially long-tenured staff writing only current duties. Push the question: what can you do that this role never asks for?
s2.transition: Profiles ready. One thing left: believing it is safe to use them.
s2.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

s3.title: Moving is normal
s3.purpose: Retire the loyalty myths and state internal mobility as a normal, encouraged Vanderbilt career path.
s3.say: None of the tooling matters if people believe using it is dangerous. So hear it stated plainly: internal mobility is a normal, encouraged career path at Vanderbilt. LinkedIn's workplace research backs it with numbers; organizations good at internal mobility keep their people nearly twice as long. A move across the university keeps your skills and your institutional knowledge here. The alternative to an internal move is usually an external one, and everybody loses that trade.
facilitate: Run Myth or normal? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round one, pause: ask who has heard that myth somewhere, show of hands or chat.
Run the breakout on what people have heard about applying internally.

ask.q: What would make you hesitate to make an internal move, honestly?
ask.respond: Name each one back to the room. The manager fear is the myth we just retired; the qualification fear is why matching runs on skills, never titles.

s3.debrief: Myths only survive in silence, and Vanderbilt is saying the opposite out loud. The numbers agree: people who can move inside an organization stay with it.
s3.watchFor: Anyone hearing this as a promise of promotions. The commitment is visibility of opportunity and safety to pursue it, never a guaranteed yes.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your next-move card.
s3.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the ask question.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One direction, in your own words: the kind of work you would say yes to. Pick the move, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Take two quiet minutes now.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with a plan started; make it real this week. Thursday's Thrive Thursday takes the next step: advocacy, the difference between a mentor who gives you advice and a sponsor who spends their credibility on you. And if you want to go deeper this month, the LinkedIn Learning course Retaining Your Best Talent by Roberta Matuson comes with a navigator-led stay-interview practice lab. See you Thursday.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone asks a Portal or Marketplace mechanics question beyond today's scope
contingencies.then: Park it visibly: 'Good question, logging it for the program team.' Point them to the Transfer Portal month materials in the series library and send parked questions upward with the pulse.

contingencies.if: A participant says their manager punishes people for looking internally
contingencies.then: Take it seriously and keep it roles-only: 'If that is happening, there are channels for it, and I will point you to them after.' Restate the policy plainly; never litigate a specific manager on the call.

toughQuestions.q: Will my manager be notified if I update my profile or get matched?
toughQuestions.a: Your profile is yours, and keeping it current is normal professional upkeep, expected of everyone this month. Best practice is to bring your named direction to your manager yourself; a manager who knows your direction can advocate for it.

toughQuestions.q: Is this just a way to move people into jobs nobody wants?
toughQuestions.a: The matching starts from your skills and your named direction, and you can always say no. Surfacing is an offer; nothing about these systems drafts anyone anywhere.

toughQuestions.q: I have been in the same role for fifteen years. Is this really for me?
toughQuestions.a: Especially for you. Long tenure usually means a deep skill set and a thin profile. The skills sweep is where fifteen years of capability finally gets written down, and stretch projects surface for exactly that depth.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Tuesday, 45 minutes to plan your next move. You know the Transfer Portal; now point it and the Talent Marketplace at your own growth. Bring one open question: what do I want next? Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the next-move plan start? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the move on your card happen? 2) What direction did you name? 3) What did your profile claim that your title never showed?
